name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Sunday 14 June 1987

clue.text: In addition, it's without the fours

indicators.note: without means lacking, so a word is dropped from the longer phrase being hinted at

blocks.note: points to plus-fours, the baggy knee-length trousers once worn for golf

explanation.surface: Someone adds a remark about a set of fours that is missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the golfing garment plus-fours and leave off the fours. The clue's it stands for the answer itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Plus is used as an adverb or conjunction meaning also, besides, in addition to that.

clue.text: Looking sympathetic and kindly, Ian moves his leg

indicators.note: moves suggests the letters are moved about into a new order

explanation.surface: A friendly-looking man named Ian shifts his leg.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan's copy reads 'lan' and has a stray full stop; the setter wrote Ian.
explanation.definitionFit: Genial describes a warm, friendly, good-natured manner, which is what sympathetic and kindly add up to.

clue.text: Hot stuff! The French have gone to Virginia

blocks.note: la is the French feminine word for the
VA is the postal abbreviation of the US state Virginia

explanation.surface: An exclamation at some sizzling news: French visitors have travelled to Virginia.
explanation.definitionFit: Lava is molten rock from a volcano, literally very hot material.

clue.text: How I worry the creature!

blocks.note: first meaning: a verb, to pester or harass someone persistently
second meaning: a burrowing black-and-white animal

explanation.walkthrough: The How I part asks for the verb in the first person: I worry, I pester.
explanation.definitionFit: To badger is to nag or harass; the badger is also a nocturnal burrowing mammal.

clue.text: Beer for tea? You do put it on!

indicators.note: the loose setter uses for as the hint that the letters are rearranged together

blocks.note: tea is spelt as the single letter it sounds like

explanation.surface: Someone is offered a beer instead of tea and told they are only pretending.
explanation.walkthrough: This old clue has no proper rearrangement signal; the letters of the drink and the single letter for tea are simply mixed. 'Put it on' pretends to mean pretend.
explanation.definitionFit: A beret is a soft round flat cap, an item of headwear you put on your head.

clue.text: Looking modest, Dee takes the rum

indicators.note: the loose setter uses this phrase to bring two words together and mix them; rum, meaning odd, hints at the disorder too

blocks.note: taken as written; a river name

explanation.surface: A modest-looking woman called Dee accepts a glass of rum.
explanation.definitionFit: Demure means reserved, shy and modest in manner or appearance.

clue.text: Regret beheading that bird?

indicators.note: beheading cuts off the head, so the opening letter of the word is removed

explanation.surface: Someone feels sorry about cutting the head off a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: An egret is a white wading heron with long plumes.

clue.text: E.T. consumed it so we must estrange him as a result

blocks.note: E.T. is the alien hero of Spielberg's 1982 film
to consume food is to eat it

explanation.surface: The film's little visitor ate something, so now we must cast him out.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan dropped the E of E.T.; the alien is the film character.
explanation.definitionFit: To alienate someone is to make them hostile or distant, the same as estranging them.

clue.text: Here's some more about the sun-god, sucker!

indicators.note: about means turned around or scattered, so the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: Ra is the Egyptian sun god

explanation.surface: Someone offers more stories about the sun god to a gullible listener.
explanation.walkthrough: Sucker looks like a gullible person; it is a fish that clings by suction.
explanation.definitionFit: The remora is a fish with a suction disc on its head that attaches it to sharks.

clue.text: How I calculate time in the East

indicators.note: the loose setter puts one word in with the other and lets them mix, with no stronger signal

explanation.surface: Someone explains how they reckon the hour while living in the Orient.
explanation.walkthrough: How I asks for the verb as I would say it: I estimate.
explanation.definitionFit: To estimate is to work out an approximate figure, a rough calculation.

clue.text: Give me lamb and I'll show you how to preserve it

indicators.note: the old-style setter promises to rework the words given, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A cook boasts they can keep a gift of lamb from spoiling.
explanation.definitionFit: To embalm is to treat a body with chemicals to preserve it from decay.

clue.text: Sounds heard from schoolgirls when you let it rest after tea

indicators.note: the old-style setter lets the words loose, so they are free to settle in a new order
after places one piece behind another in the answer

blocks.note: tea is spelt as the single letter it sounds like

explanation.surface: Girls at school giggle when told to leave the dishes to rest after tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Titters are nervous, half-suppressed giggles, the stereotyped noise of schoolgirls.

clue.text: Your tie has a tear in it? Say that again!

indicators.note: the loose setter joins two words with has and lets their letters mix, a tear hinting at damage

explanation.surface: Someone, hearing that your necktie is ripped, asks you to repeat yourself in disbelief.
explanation.definitionFit: To iterate is to repeat, to do or say something once more.

clue.text: I see, even this can show it clearly

indicators.note: the old-style setter asks what these letters can become once put in a new order
see is a spoken word whose sound stands for a single letter

blocks.note: the word sounds like the name of the letter

explanation.surface: Someone realises that even this can make things plain.
explanation.definitionFit: To evince is to reveal or display a quality or feeling plainly.

clue.text: Being somewhat heavy, I sat out at the ball

definitions.note: the answer is a noun, a heavy load; the clue describes it

indicators.note: out means disordered or out of place, so the letters beside it change places

explanation.surface: A rather plump guest admits to sitting out the dances at the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: it describes the answer as heavy matter rather than naming it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballast is heavy material carried low in a ship to keep it steady.

clue.text: A dance a minute!

indicators.note: the exclamation mark is the old-style setter's only hint that the word that follows must be rearranged

explanation.surface: An exclamation that a dance lasts only sixty seconds.
explanation.definitionFit: The minuet is a slow, stately ballroom dance in triple time from the 17th century.

clue.text: One way to sneer at that which is considered to be oriental

indicators.note: one way of writing the letters means one arrangement among many possible orders

linkWords: that which is considered to be

explanation.surface: A remark about showing contempt for anything thought to come from the Orient.
explanation.definitionFit: Oriental and eastern both describe things from Asia, the lands to the east.

clue.text: Shirley has a place to say her prayers

definitions.text: a place to say her prayers

blocks.note: first meaning: the surname of Shirley ..., the 1930s Hollywood child star

blocks.clueFragment: a place to say her prayers
blocks.note: second meaning: a building for worship

explanation.walkthrough: Shirley alone stands for her famous surname, an allusion rather than a strict definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A temple is a building devoted to worship, where people go to pray.

clue.text: Give the Scotsman it or the lizard will get it

blocks.note: mon is the Scots form of man

explanation.surface: A threat: hand it to the Scot, or else the lizard will have it.
explanation.definitionFit: Monitors are a genus of large lizards, including the Komodo dragon.

clue.text: Most cope with the sun-god in such a presentation

indicators.note: most of a word is all but part of it, here losing its opening letter

blocks.note: Ra is the Egyptian sun god

explanation.surface: Performers mostly manage when the Egyptian sun god appears in the show.
explanation.walkthrough: Most usually removes the last letter; here the first is dropped. Verdi's Aida, set in Egypt, makes the sun god apt.
explanation.definitionFit: An opera is a staged drama set to music, a kind of theatrical presentation.

clue.text: So is a fertile spot developed

indicators.note: something developed has been worked into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A note that a piece of fertile ground has likewise been built on.
explanation.definitionFit: An oasis is a fertile area in a desert where water is found.

clue.text: Get together and I'll show you this mess of a bale

indicators.note: the old-style setter promises to rework the words given, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: An invitation to come together and see what a muddle a bale of hay is.
explanation.walkthrough: Mess is both a word in the fodder and a hint of disorder; 'of a' just joins it to the other word.
explanation.definitionFit: To assemble is to gather or come together in one place.

clue.text: So twice you say it's tolerable

explanation.surface: A shrug: say it twice and it becomes just about acceptable.
explanation.definitionFit: So-so means middling, neither good nor bad, merely passable.

clue.text: Most of the flute can be played differently

definitions.note: the answer is a noun; the clue describes it as an instrument

indicators.note: most of a word is all but part of it, here losing its opening letter

explanation.surface: Remarks that much of a flute could be played another way.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: the answer is another instrument, one plucked rather than blown.
explanation.definitionFit: A lute is a plucked string instrument with a pear-shaped body, played very unlike a woodwind.

clue.text: It keeps coming back although we give it the right cures

indicators.note: the loose setter offers a treatment of the letters, which here means reordering them

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A disease keeps returning despite our proper remedies.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that recurs happens again and again, returning repeatedly.

clue.text: It keeps ale in the sun if we detach it like this

definitions.text: It keeps ale in the sun
definitions.note: describes what the answer does rather than naming the act

blocks.clueFragment: It keeps ale in the sun
blocks.note: first meaning: to wrap something to stop heat getting in, as with a cool box for beer
second meaning: to cut off or isolate from surroundings

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a playful description of keeping drinks cool, the second the sense of setting something apart.
explanation.definitionFit: To insulate is to protect from heat transfer, and also to isolate or cut off from outside influences.

clue.text: 100 Romans perform for us in the desert

definitions.note: describes where the answer grows rather than naming it

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral for 100

explanation.surface: A hundred Romans put on a show for us out in the desert.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: it names where the plant is found rather than the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Cacti are spiny succulent plants characteristic of arid deserts.
